mainTopic: A Jew's ox goring a gentile's ox: the sources, the reward of בני נח, the Roman officers, and עולא's words of comfort
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion about why ״רֵעֵהוּ״ was written by a תם. Then the גמרא quotes the משנה: a Jew's ox that gores a gentile's ox is exempt, but a gentile's ox that gores a Jew's ox pays in full. It asks a ממה נפשך: whichever way you read ״רֵעֵהוּ״, both directions should come out the same. רבי אבהו answers from a פסוק in חבקוק, and רבי יוחנן answers from ״הוֹפִיעַ מֵהַר פָּארָן״. A ברייתא quotes both פסוקים, and the גמרא explains that the second is needed because the חבקוק פסוק may be used for the teachings of רב מתנה (exile) and רב יוסף (the nations' מצוות were 'released'). The גמרא concludes that the nations still get reward for keeping their מצוות, but only like one who is not commanded, since גדול המצווה ועושה. Next comes the story of Roman officers who accepted the whole תורה except this law of the ox. The amud ends with עולא comforting רב שמואל בר יהודה, whose lesson about משה and מואב continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the word 'of another' was written by an unwarned ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes an earlier argument. If the exemption covered every case, the תורה would have written ״רֵעֵהוּ״ by the מועד, a warned ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because if that were so, the verse should have written this word "of another" in the section about a warned ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing an earlier argument by pointing to where the תורה chose to write the word ״רֵעֵהוּ״.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim is that a full exemption would have been taught by a מועד, the stricter case. From there we would learn the תם, the lighter case, through a קל וחומר. Since the תורה wrote ״רֵעֵהוּ״ by the תם, the exemption must be narrower than a complete exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: Because if so: introduces what would follow if the other view were true
His fellow / of another: the key word in the פסוק about oxen goring
A warned ox: one known to gore, whose owner pays full damages

phrases.english: Because if so, let the verse write
this word "of another" in the case of a warned ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִם כֵּן, נִכְתּוֹב קְרָא לְהַאי ״רֵעֵהוּ״ גַּבֵּי מוּעָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the earlier discussion about an ox of הקדש, which comes before this part.
steps.raayaObject: That the exemption learned from ״רֵעֵהוּ״ is not a complete exemption in every case
steps.raayaSupportSource: Where the תורה placed the word ״רֵעֵהוּ״: by the תם rather than by the מועד

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: a Jew's ox that gores a gentile's ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to a new line in the משנה: a Jew's ox that gores a gentile's ox is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: An ox of a Jew that gored the ox of a gentile: the owner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling to set up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules one way here and the opposite way in the reverse case. When a gentile's ox gores a Jew's ox, the owner pays full damages. The next step points out that these two rulings seem to pull against each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt: does not have to pay

phrases.english: An ox of a Jew that gored
the ox of a gentile – is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹר שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנָּגַח שׁוֹר שֶׁל גּוֹי – פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A Jew's ox that gores a gentile's ox: the owner is exempt (and in the reverse case he pays in full).

steps.title: Whichever way you read 'of another', the ruling is hard
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים argue that both readings of ״רֵעֵהוּ״ fail. If it is exact, the gentile should also be exempt. If it is not exact, the Jew should also be liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: whichever way you look at it there is a problem. If "of another" is meant exactly, then when a gentile's ox gores a Jew's ox, he should also be exempt. And if "of another" is not meant exactly, then even when a Jew's ox gores a gentile's ox, he should be liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the משנה's two-sided ruling with a ממה נפשך argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If ״רֵעֵהוּ״ limits the law to a fellow Jew, then the law of goring should not apply between a Jew and a gentile at all, in either direction. If it does not limit, the law should apply in both directions. Either way, the two cases should come out the same, yet the משנה treats them differently.

keyTerms.meaning: They said: the חכמים raised the point
Whichever way you want: both options lead to a problem
Not exactly: not meant to limit

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not about either ruling by itself. It is about why the two directions are treated differently, when one reading of the word should cover both.

phrases.english: They said: whichever way you look at it,
if "of another" is meant exactly –
then a gentile's ox, when it gores
a Jew's ox, should also be exempt!
And if "of another" is not meant exactly –
then even a Jew's ox,
when it gores a gentile's ox, should be liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling just quoted from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's different treatment of a Jew's ox goring a gentile's ox and a gentile's ox goring a Jew's ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A single reading of ״רֵעֵהוּ″ should give the same result in both directions: either both are exempt or both are liable.

steps.title: רבי אבהו: the source is a פסוק in חבקוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו reads a פסוק in חבקוק to mean that because the בני נח did not keep their שבע מצוות‎, ה׳ permitted their money to ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: the verse says, "He stood and shook the earth; He saw and made the nations tremble." He saw the seven מצוות that the descendants of Noah accepted upon themselves. Since they did not keep them, He arose and permitted their money to the Jewish people.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו answers the challenge with a source from a פסוק in חבקוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference between the two directions does not come from the word ״רֵעֵהוּ״. It comes from a separate source. רבי אבהו reads וַיַּתֵּר as "permitted": because the nations did not keep the שבע מצוות בני נח, their money was permitted, so a Jew is not liable in this case.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse says: introduces a source from a פסוק
The seven commandments given to all of humanity

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said: the verse says:
"He stood and shook the earth,
He saw and made the nations tremble" –
phrases.notes: The גמרא reads וַיַּתֵּר as if it came from הִתִּיר, "permitted."

phrases.english: He saw the seven מצוות
that the descendants of Noah accepted upon themselves.
Since they did not keep them –
He arose and permitted their money to the Jewish people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ממה נפשך challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a separate verse that explains the difference between the two directions
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole ruling depends only on how to read ״רֵעֵהוּ″, so both directions must come out the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: A separate source, the פסוק in חבקוק, explains why a Jew is exempt when his ox gores a gentile's ox.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: a different source from הר פארן
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן brings a different פסוק: "He appeared from הר פארן," read as "from פארן their money was revealed to ישראל."
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: the source is from here: "He appeared from הר פארן". From פארן their money appeared, given to ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a second, different source for the same ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees with the ruling but finds it in a פסוק in דברים about the giving of the תורה. He reads הוֹפִיעַ, "appeared," as saying that from פארן the nations' money was revealed and given to ישראל.

keyTerms.meaning: From here: introduces a different source
Mount Paran, mentioned in the פסוק about the giving of the תורה

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's two-way ruling is explained by a separate source, not by the word ״רֵעֵהוּ״. רבי אבהו learns it from חבקוק (the nations did not keep the שבע מצוות), and רבי יוחנן learns it from "He appeared from הר פארן."

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said: from here:
"He appeared from Mount Paran" –
from Paran their money appeared, given to the Jewish people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different source for the same answer that רבי אבהו gave.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Another verse brought as the source for the same ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The source is the פסוק in חבקוק that רבי אבהו cited.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling can also be learned from "He appeared from Mount Paran."

steps.title: A ברייתא backs up the rule and both פסוקים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same rule: a Jew's ox that gores a gentile's ox is exempt. A gentile's ox that gores a Jew's ox pays full damage, whether תם or מועד. It quotes both the פסוק from חבקוק and the פסוק about פארן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches this too: if a Jew's ox gores a gentile's ox, the owner is exempt. If a gentile's ox gores a Jew's ox, the owner pays full damage, whether the ox is a תם or a מועד. The source is ״He stood and shook the earth, He saw and released the nations.״ It also says: ״He appeared from Mount פארן.״
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports the rule it has been explaining. This ברייתא uses the same two פסוקים that רבי אבהו and רבי יוחנן used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא repeats the משנה's ruling, including that a gentile's ox pays full damage even when it is a תם, which normally pays only half. What it adds is the source from the פסוקים: it quotes both the פסוק from חבקוק and the פסוק about פארן. That sets up the next question: why does it need both?

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא also teaches this, bringing support
An ox that is not known to gore; it normally pays half damage
An ox known to gore after being warned; it pays full damage

phrases.english: This is also taught in a ברייתא:
An ox of a Jew that gored
the ox of a gentile – is exempt.
An ox of a gentile that gored
the ox of a Jew –

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין תָּם בֵּין מוּעָד מְשַׁלֵּם נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם,
phrases.english: whether innocuous or forewarned, pays full damage,
as it is said: "He stood and shook the earth,
He saw, and released the nations."
And it says: "He appeared from Mount Paran."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answers of רבי אבהו and רבי יוחנן with a ברייתא that uses both of their פסוקים.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a Jew's ox goring a gentile's ox is exempt, and that a gentile pays full damage.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting חבקוק 3:6 and דברים 33:2.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא need a second פסוק?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא adds ״and it says,״ bringing a second פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of ״and it says״?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא brings a second פסוק when it already gave one. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״וְאוֹמֵר״ means a second source is coming. That suggests the first source was not enough on its own. The גמרא wants to know what was missing from the first פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: "And it says," which introduces an extra פסוק

phrases.english: What is the reason for "and it says"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the structure of the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the first פסוק is not enough, so that a second one is needed.

steps.title: The first פסוק may be used up for other teachings
steps.stepSummary: Someone might say the חבקוק פסוק is needed for the teachings of רב מתנה and רב יוסף. So the ברייתא adds the פארן פסוק as a clear source.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the פסוק ״He stood and shook the earth״ is needed for what רב מתנה and רב יוסף learn from it, come and hear: ״He appeared from Mount פארן״ means from פארן their money was revealed to ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the second פסוק covers a gap. The first פסוק might be needed for a different teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פסוק that is already used for one teaching may not be free to teach a second law. Since the חבקוק פסוק may be taken by רב מתנה and רב יוסף, the ברייתא backs itself up with the פארן פסוק, which clearly teaches the money law.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say, which raises a possible objection
It is needed for something else
Come and hear, which brings a source

phrases.english: And if you would say, this "He stood and shook the earth" –

phrases.aramaic: מִבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ לְכִדְרַב מַתְנָה וְכִדְרַב יוֹסֵף,
phrases.english: is needed for what רב מתנה and רב יוסף teach,
come and hear: "He appeared from Mount Paran" –
from Paran their money was revealed to ישראל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why the ברייתא needed ״וְאוֹמֵר״.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first פסוק might be used for the teachings of רב מתנה and רב יוסף, so the second פסוק secures the money law.

steps.title: רב מתנה‎: ה׳ exiled the nations for not keeping their מצוות
steps.stepSummary: רב מתנה explains that ה׳ saw the בני נח did not keep their שבע מצוות, so He exiled them from their land.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רב מתנה's teaching? רב מתנה said: ״He stood and shook the earth, He saw...״ What did He see? He saw the seven מצוות that the בני נח were commanded and did not keep. So He rose and exiled them from their land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the רב מתנה teaching it just mentioned. This shows what else the חבקוק פסוק could be used for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב מתנה reads ״וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם״ as exile, not as permitting money. That is why the פסוק might not be free to teach the money law. רב יוסף's teaching is explained in steps 12-13.

keyTerms.meaning: The seven commandments given to all humanity

phrases.english: What is the teaching of רב מתנה?
As רב מתנה said:
"He stood and shook the earth, He saw, etc."
What did He see –
He saw the seven מצוות

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנִּצְטַוּוּ עֲלֵיהֶן בְּנֵי נֹחַ וְלֹא קִיְּימוּם,
phrases.english: that the descendants of Noah were commanded and did not keep,
He arose and exiled them from their land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the רב מתנה teaching mentioned in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ״וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם״ means ה׳ exiled the nations because they did not keep the שבע מצוות.

steps.title: How do we know ״וַיַּתֵּר״ means exile?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that the word ״וַיַּתֵּר״ is a word for exile.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know that this word ״וַיַּתֵּר״ means exile?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how רב מתנה knows that ״וַיַּתֵּר״ means exile. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי אבהו read ״וַיַּתֵּר״ as permitting. רב מתנה reads it as exile, so the גמרא wants proof of that meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: And how is it implied, a request for proof

phrases.english: And from where is it implied
that this word "vayyatter" is a term of exile?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי מַשְׁמַע דְּהַאי ״וַיַּתֵּר״ לִישָּׁנָא דְּאִגַּלּוֹיֵי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the word meaning that רב מתנה's teaching depends on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that ״וַיַּתֵּר״ means exile.

steps.title: ״לְנַתֵּר״ means to leap, so ״וַיַּתֵּר״ means uprooting
steps.stepSummary: The same root appears in ״לְנַתֵּר״, which the Aramaic translation renders as ״to leap.״ So the root means moving from one place to another, which is exile.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is written ״וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם,״ and there it is written ״לְנַתֵּר upon the earth,״ which we translate into Aramaic as ״to leap upon the earth.״
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the meaning of ״וַיַּתֵּר״ by comparing it to the same root in another פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ויקרא, ״לְנַתֵּר״ describes locusts leaping, and the Aramaic translation says ״לְקַפָּצָא״, to jump. Jumping means leaving one spot for another, so ״וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם״ means ה׳ made the nations leave their land, which is exile.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written here... and it is written there, comparing two פסוקים
And we translate it into Aramaic

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא needs two פסוקים because the חבקוק פסוק might be used for other teachings. One is רב מתנה's: ״וַיַּתֵּר״ means exile, as in ״לְנַתֵּר״, to leap. The other is רב יוסף's, explained in the next steps. The פארן פסוק clearly teaches the money law.

phrases.english: It is written here: "And made the nations vayyatter,"
and it is written there: "Lenatter with them upon the earth" –
and we translate it: "To leap with them upon the earth."
phrases.notes: Leaping means moving from one place to another, which is the idea of exile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10's question about the meaning of ״וַיַּתֵּר״.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The root נתר means leaping, as the Aramaic translation of ״לְנַתֵּר״ shows, so ״וַיַּתֵּר״ means uprooting the nations from their land.

steps.title: What is רב יוסף's teaching?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב יוסף's teaching on the פסוק is, since step 8 only mentioned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the teaching of רב יוסף?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא already explained רב מתנה's teaching. Now it asks what the second teaching, from רב יוסף, says. This line sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8 the גמרא said the חבקוק פסוק is needed for two teachings: רב מתנה's and רב יוסף's. רב מתנה's was given in step 9. Now the גמרא turns to the second one.

phrases.english: What is the teaching of Rav Yosef?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רב מתנה's teaching (steps 9-11) to the second teaching promised in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The content of רב יוסף's teaching on the חבקוק פסוק.

steps.title: ה׳ released the seven מצוות from the nations
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that ה׳ saw בני נח did not keep their שבע מצוות, so He 'released' those מצוות from them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: 'He stood and shook the earth, He saw...' What did He see? He saw the seven מצוות that בני נח accepted and did not keep. So He stood and released them from those מצוות.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains the same פסוק differently from רב מתנה. He reads the word ויתר as 'released' or 'permitted.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב מתנה, ויתר meant exile. For רב יוסף, it means ה׳ 'untied' the מצוות, so the nations were released from them. This reading is surprising, and the next step questions it.

keyTerms.meaning: The seven commandments given to all mankind
Descendants of Noach, meaning all the nations

phrases.english: As Rav Yosef said:
"He stood and shook the earth, He saw, etc."
phrases.notes: חבקוק 3:6. The 'etc.' points to the next words, וַיַּתֵּר גּוֹיִם, which רב יוסף is about to explain.

phrases.english: What did He see?
He saw the seven commandments
that the descendants of Noach accepted upon themselves
and did not keep them,
so He stood and released them from them.
phrases.notes: Here רב יוסף reads וַיַּתֵּר as 'released' (like מַתִּיר), not as exile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12 by quoting רב יוסף's reading of the פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ויתר means ה׳ released the nations from their seven מצוות because they did not keep them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because בני נח failed to keep their seven מצוות‎, ה׳ 'released' those מצוות from them.

steps.title: Would sinners end up gaining?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף: if their מצוות were released, the sinners came out ahead, and a sinner would be rewarded.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did they profit from this? If so, we have found a sinner who is rewarded!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב יוסף's teaching. It is strange that people who broke the rules would get freed from those rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being released from מצוות sounds like a prize. Sinning should not earn a prize. So the גמרא needs to understand 'released' in some other way.

phrases.english: Did they really profit?!
If so, we have found a sinner who is rewarded!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the logic of רב יוסף's teaching from step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's statement that ה׳ released the nations from their מצוות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Releasing someone from obligations because he sinned would mean the sinner benefits, which makes no sense.

steps.title: Released means no reward for keeping them
steps.stepSummary: מר בריה דרבנא explains that 'released' does not mean they may now break the מצוות. It means that even if they keep them, they get no reward.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר son of רבנא said: It means that even if they keep them, they do not get reward for them.
steps.whatsHappening: מר בריה דרבנא answers the challenge. 'Released' is a loss for the nations, not a gain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nations are still forbidden to break the seven מצוות. What they lost is the reward for keeping them. So the sinner does not gain; he loses.

phrases.english: Mar, son of Rabbana, said:
It comes to say that even if they keep them,
they do not get reward for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: the meaning of 'released' is redefined.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Released' means the nations may now freely break the seven מצוות, which would be a gain.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Released' means they lose the reward for keeping them, which is a punishment.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the nations are now allowed to break the seven מצוות. They are still bound by them; only the reward was taken away.

steps.title: Challenge: a גוי who learns תורה is like a כהן גדול
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that a גוי gets no reward, using רבי מאיר's ברייתא that a גוי who learns Torah is like a כהן גדול.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do they really get no reward? But a ברייתא teaches that רבי מאיר says: How do we know that even a גוי who learns תורה is like a כהן גדול? The פסוק says, 'which a person shall do and live by them.' It does not say כהנים, לויים and ישראלים, but 'a person.' So you learn that even a גוי who learns תורה is like a כהן גדול!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges מר בריה דרבנא's answer. A ברייתא seems to show that a גוי does get great reward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר learns from the word 'אדם' (a person) that the פסוק includes everyone, not just Jews. If a גוי can reach the level of a כהן גדול, he clearly gets reward. That contradicts the claim that the nations get no reward at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And he shall live by them

phrases.english: And do they not get reward?!
But a ברייתא teaches: Rabbi Meir says:
From where do we know that even a gentile who learns Torah
is like a High Priest?
The verse says:
"Which a person shall do, and live by them"
It does not say "Kohanim, Levi'im and Yisraelim,"
but rather "a person";

phrases.aramaic: הָא לָמַדְתָּ, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ גּוֹי וְעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה –
phrases.english: so you have learned that even a gentile who learns Torah
is like a High Priest!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of מר בריה דרבנא in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: מר בריה דרבנא's claim that the nations get no reward for keeping the מצוות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי מאיר shows from the word 'אדם' that a גוי who learns Torah reaches the level of a כהן גדול, which means he must get reward.

steps.title: They get reward, but a smaller kind
steps.stepSummary: The answer: a גוי does get reward, but only like someone who is not commanded and does it anyway. רבי חנינא teaches that someone who is commanded and does is greater.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: They do not get reward like someone who is commanded and does. They get reward like someone who is not commanded and does. As רבי חנינא said: Someone who is commanded and does is greater than someone who is not commanded and does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from רבי מאיר by clarifying what 'no reward' meant. It backs this up with רבי חנינא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'No reward' did not mean zero reward. It meant they lost the higher reward of someone who is commanded. Since the מצוות were 'released,' the nations are now treated like volunteers, and a volunteer's reward is smaller. This fits both רב יוסף and רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who is commanded and does it
Someone who is not commanded but does it anyway
The אמורא whose rule backs up the answer

steps.whatToRemember: The nations were not freed to sin. They lost the higher reward of being 'commanded,' so they now get only the reward of a volunteer. As רבי חנינא says, גדול המצווה ועושה.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבי חנינא's rule, that someone who is commanded and does is greater than someone who is not commanded and does, is a famous rule used across ש״ס.

phrases.english: They said: They do not get reward for them
like one who is commanded and does,
but like one who is not commanded and does.
As Rabbi Chanina said:
Greater is one who is commanded and does
than one who is not commanded and does.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: אֵין מְקַבְּלִים עֲלֵיהֶן שָׂכָר כִּמְצֻוֶּוה וְעוֹשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 by refining the answer of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Refinement: 'no reward' is narrowed to mean 'no reward of one who is commanded.'
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The nations get no reward at all for keeping their מצוות.
steps.terutzMaskana: They get the smaller reward of one who is not commanded and does, so רבי מאיר's ברייתא still holds.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: After the 'release,' the nations' keeping of the מצוות earns the reward of one who is not commanded, which is less than the reward of one who is commanded, as רבי חנינא teaches.

steps.title: Roman officers study the תורה and question one law
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how two Roman officers learned the whole תורה three times. They said it was all true except the law about a Jew's ox and a גוי's ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: The Roman government once sent two officers to the חכמי ישראל and said, 'Teach us your תורה.' They read it, repeated it, and read it a third time. When they were leaving, they said: 'We examined your whole תורה and it is true, except for one thing you say. If a Jew's ox gores a גוי's ox, the owner is exempt. If a גוי's ox gores a Jew's ox, whether it is a תם or a מועד, the owner pays full damage.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story (a ברייתא) connected to the law on our daf about a גוי's ox. Here the officers state the one law they find hard to accept.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The officers praise the entire תורה, which makes their single complaint stand out. They describe the law as uneven: the Jew is exempt in one direction, but the גוי pays in full in the other direction, even for a תם.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; this opens a ברייתא
Officers or officials of the government
An ox that has not yet built a pattern of goring; it normally pays only half damage
An ox that has been warned for goring repeatedly; it pays full damage

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
And once the Roman kingdom sent
two officers to the Sages of Israel, saying:
Teach us your Torah.
They read it, repeated it, and went over it a third time.
When they were leaving, they said to them:
We examined your whole Torah, and it is true;
except for this one thing that you say:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנָּגַח שׁוֹר שֶׁל גּוֹי – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: A Jew's ox that gored a gentile's ox is exempt.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁל גּוֹי שֶׁנָּגַח שׁוֹר שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל –
phrases.english: But a gentile's ox that gored a Jew's ox,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין תָּם בֵּין מוּעָד, מְשַׁלֵּם נֶזֶק שָׁלֵם.
phrases.english: whether it is innocuous or forewarned, pays full damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן, וּכְבָר שָׁלְחָה מַלְכוּת רוֹמִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the discussion of reward for בני נח to a ברייתא story about the law of a גוי's ox from earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The officers accept the whole Torah except the law that a Jew's ox goring a גוי's ox is exempt, while a גוי's ox goring a Jew's ox pays full damage.

steps.title: The officers' 'whichever way you look at it' argument
steps.stepSummary: The officers argue that the word רעהו either limits the law to Jews on both sides or it does not. Either way, the law should be the same in both directions.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whichever way you look at it: if 'his fellow' is meant exactly (only Jews), then even a גוי's ox that gores a Jew's ox should be exempt. If 'his fellow' is not meant exactly (it includes everyone), then even a Jew's ox that gores a גוי's ox should be liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The officers explain why they find the law difficult. They show that it does not fit either way of reading the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose רעהו means only a fellow Jew. Then a גוי is outside this law completely, and should not pay either. Suppose רעהו includes everyone. Then the Jew should pay too. The current law seems to take one reading for one side and the other reading for the other side.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you take it; an 'either way' argument
His fellow; the word in the פסוק about oxen that gore

steps.confusionAlert: This argument is the officers' complaint, not the גמרא's conclusion. The ברייתא tells it as their objection, and the explanation behind the law was given earlier on the daf.

phrases.english: Whichever way you look at it:
If 'his fellow' is meant exactly,
phrases.notes: This is the word in שמות 21:35, where a person's ox gores the ox of 'his fellow.'

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ דְּגוֹי כִּי נָגַח דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לִיפְּטַר;
phrases.english: then even when a gentile's ox gores a Jew's ox, he should be exempt;
and if 'his fellow' is not meant exactly,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ דְיִשְׂרָאֵל כִּי נָגַח דְּגוֹי לִחַיַּיב!
phrases.english: then even when a Jew's ox gores a gentile's ox, he should be liable!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the officers' complaint from step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The uneven law of a Jew's ox and a גוי's ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An either-way argument: each possible reading of רעהו should give the same result in both directions.

steps.title: The officers will not report it to the government
steps.stepSummary: The officers promise not to tell the Roman government about this law.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we will not tell this matter to the government.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the officers deciding to keep this law to themselves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They had just said the whole תורה is true, so they choose not to report the one law that might anger the government.
steps.whatToRemember: The Roman officers called the תורה true but struggled with the law of a גוי's ox. They kept that law from the government.

phrases.aramaic: וְדָבָר זֶה אֵין אָנוּ מוֹדִיעִים אוֹתוֹ לַמַּלְכוּת.
phrases.english: And this matter we will not report to the government.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדָבָר זֶה אֵין אָנוּ מוֹדִיעִים אוֹתוֹ לַמַּלְכוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the story of the officers.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The officers chose not to report this law to the government.

steps.title: עולא refuses to join the Babylonian way of comforting mourners
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר יהודה's daughter died. עולא would not go with רבנן to comfort him, because the Babylonians say 'What can one do?' He called this גידופא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The daughter of רב שמואל בר יהודה died. The Rabbis said to עולא: 'Come, let's go comfort him.' He said to them: 'What do I have to do with the comforting of the Babylonians, which is גידופא? They say, "What can one do?" That suggests that if it were possible to do something, they would do it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story. עולא explains why he will not comfort the mourner together with the רבנן of בבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'What can one do?' sounds as if we accept ה׳'s decree only because we have no choice. עולא hears it as suggesting that we would go against ה׳'s decree if we could. To him, that is disrespectful to ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: Words of comfort for a mourner

phrases.aramaic: רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה שְׁכִיבָא לֵיהּ בְּרַתָּא,
phrases.english: The daughter of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda died.
The Rabbis said to Ulla:
Get up, let us go comfort him.
He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי אִית לִי גַּבֵּי נֶחָמְתָּא דְבַבְלָאֵי –
phrases.english: What do I have to do with the comforting of the Babylonians,
which is blasphemy?
For they say: 'What can one do?'
This implies that if it were possible to do something, they would do it.
phrases.notes: He means they would act against ה׳'s decree if they could.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה שְׁכִיבָא לֵיהּ בְּרַתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story that moves away from the law of the ox.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עולא objects to the Babylonian phrase of comfort, 'What can one do?', as disrespectful to ה׳.

steps.title: עולא asks why משה needed to be warned about מואב
steps.stepSummary: עולא goes alone to comfort the mourner. He quotes the פסוק telling משה not to fight מואב and asks why משה would ever have thought of going to war without permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא went to him by himself and said to him: 'The פסוק says, "ה׳ said to משה: Do not harass מואב and do not start a war with them." What was משה thinking? Would he have gone to war without permission?!'
steps.whatsHappening: עולא begins his own words of comfort by asking a question on a פסוק. He is setting up a lesson that will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳ warned משה not to fight מואב, which suggests משה was planning to do so. That seems strange, because משה would never fight without ה׳'s permission. So עולא asks what משה was really thinking.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not harass, do not be hostile
Do not provoke, do not start a fight

phrases.english: He went to him by himself.
He said to him:
'And ה׳ said (to Moshe):
phrases.notes: דברים 2:9. The פסוק itself says 'to me' (משה is speaking), so some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

phrases.english: Do not harass Moab,
and do not start a war with them.'

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מָה עָלָה עַל דַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה,
phrases.english: What, then, entered Moshe's mind?
To make war without permission?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מָה עָלָה עַל דַּעְתּוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: עולא, having refused to go with the others, now goes alone and begins his own comfort.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why משה needed a warning not to fight מואב, since he would never fight without permission.

steps.title: משה's own קל וחומר about the מדינים
steps.stepSummary: עולא answers that משה made a קל וחומר by himself. If the תורה commanded war against the מדינים, who only came to help מואב, then surely מואב should be attacked too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, משה made a קל וחומר on his own. He said: 'The מדינים only came to help מואב, and yet the תורה said, "Harass the מדינים and strike them"...'
steps.whatsHappening: עולא answers his own question. משה was not acting on his own will; he was reasoning from a law the תורה had already given. The reasoning continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה compared the two nations. The מדינים were only helpers, yet they were to be attacked. So מואב, the main troublemaker, should be attacked even more. This explains why ה׳ had to tell him not to.

keyTerms.meaning: A reasoning from a lighter case to a stronger case
Made, carried out (a line of reasoning)

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא נָשָׂא מֹשֶׁה קַל וָחוֹמֶר בְּעַצְמוֹ –
phrases.english: Rather, Moshe made a kal vachomer by himself.
He said: If the Midianites,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא בָּאוּ אֶלָּא לַעֲזוֹר אֶת מוֹאָב,
phrases.english: who came only to help Moab,
the Torah said about them:
'Harass the Midianites and strike them,'
phrases.notes: במדבר 25:17. The sentence is not finished yet; the second half of משה's reasoning comes next.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא נָשָׂא מֹשֶׁה קַל וָחוֹמֶר בְּעַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: משה reasoned with a קל וחומר from the command to attack the מדינים, who were only helpers, that מואב should be attacked as well.
